title: Mail on Sunday ends up funding state school scholarship via payout to MP
summary:
Labour’s Catherine Atkinson says she will give students £5,000 paid to her by paper that falsely accused her of concealing private school education

A new scholarship supporting state-educated students will be inadvertently funded by the Mail on Sunday (MoS), using a payout it made after being threatened with legal action by the Labour MP Catherine Atkinson.

The Derby North MP says she will use the proceeds of about £5,000 from the newspaper to fund scholarships for local law students at the University of Derby who – like her – attended state schools.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A new scholarship supporting state-educated students will be inadvertently funded by the Mail on Sunday (MoS), using a payout it made after being threatened with legal action by the Labour MP Catherine Atkinson.

The Derby North MP says she will use the proceeds of about £5,000 from the newspaper to fund scholarships for local law students at the University of Derby who – like her – attended state schools.

In early July the MoS said Atkinson attended a private school and accused her of concealing it from her biographical entry in Who’s Who.

Despite Atkinson correcting the journalists who contacted her, the MoS published an article making the false claim, accompanied by a large photograph of the MP. The newspaper later apologised and paid damages and legal costs after the former lawyer responded firmly that she had attended state schools.

“I am grateful for the state-school education that helped me build a 17-year career as a barrister,” said Atkinson, who attended Sacred Heart high school, a Catholic comprehensive in Hammersmith, west London.

“The claim that I had concealed a private education from my constituents was false. I am using the money from this settlement to support students from Derby’s state schools in beginning their own careers in law.

“Strengthening our justice system means taking seriously who gets the opportunity to work in it. When financial barriers keep capable people out of the profession, the public loses the benefit of their talent.

“The legal profession has a shared responsibility to help remove those barriers. We should be looking for future lawyers in every school and supporting those who need help to get started.

“There are students in Derby today who could spend their careers defending the rights of others. They deserve the opportunity to build that future.”

Atkinson was elected at the 2024 general election as MP for Derby North, where the University of Derby’s law school is situated.

At least £5,000 from the settlement after expenses will go towards the Catherine Atkinson future lawyers award, providing a £500 award each year for at least 10 years. The award will be open to first-year law students who were educated at a state school within the city of Derby.

Prof Kathryn Mitchell, the university’s vice-chancellor, said she welcomed Atkinson’s support.

Mitchell said: “At the University of Derby we firmly believe in the transformative nature of education and, as a champion of social mobility and inclusion, aim to create opportunities for all across our region and beyond, regardless of age, background or location.

“We want talented students from Derby’s state comprehensive schools to have every opportunity to pursue a career in law.

“The Catherine Atkinson future lawyers award will provide financial support as recipients begin their degrees. We welcome Catherine’s commitment to social mobility and her investment in local students over the next 10 years.”

title: The Enrollment Wins of 2026
summary:
The Enrollment Wins of 2026 Johanna Alonso Fri, 09/11/2026 - 03:00 AM Several colleges cited partnerships with K–12 schools and new, dedicated analyses of enrollment data as key elements of their enrollment booms. Byline(s) Johanna Alonso The Enrollment Wins of 2026
Johanna Alonso Fri, 09/11/2026 - 03:00 AM

Several colleges cited partnerships with K–12 schools and new, dedicated analyses of enrollment data as key elements of their enrollment booms.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
It’s a weird time for higher education. Enrollment is increasing over all, with many flagship universities, highly selective colleges and community colleges appearing to have no difficulty filling seats.

Yet other institutions are struggling to meet their enrollment goals, especially as international student numbers continue to dip, potential students opt to enter the workforce or seek credentials outside higher ed, and the number of high school graduates begins to decrease each year.

Still, a slate of institutions reached new enrollment records this year, in some cases capitalizing on momentum while others reversed years of declines or stagnation. There is no one strategy that each institution employed, but many focused on strengthening local recruitment pathways, adding high-demand programs and launching unique recruitment efforts.

These six institutions are among the success stories of fall 2026: colleges and universities that have found ways to stand out from the crowd and attract new students.

Southern Illinois University Edwardsville

Located in the greater St. Louis area, SIUE had a long history as a commuter campus, which made expanding enrollment difficult. But 2026 marks the second fall in a row that it saw a major enrollment bump; combined, total enrollment has increased by almost 15 percent. First-year enrollment surged by 50 percent in that same span.

SIUE’s Students Taking Action for Registration and Transition program—SIUE START for short—provided a major pipeline to the institution from local high schools. Through the program, SIUE staff brought placement testing, academic advising and course registration directly into 10 nearby high schools, helping students overcome obstacles in the enrollment process.

“Students graduated with their college schedule, an early connection to their SIUE advising team, and a clearer understanding of what came next,” Nicole Franklin, the institution’s director of communications, wrote in an email. “It was a practical way to resolve challenges before they became barriers to enrollment.”

SIUE hopes to expand the program in the coming years. The college is also focused on improving sophomore retention by introducing interventions like tutoring and success coaching “earlier, more often, and more consistently into the student experience” so that students are familiar and comfortable with those offerings before they need them, according to Franklin. Also as part of the focus on retention, the institution’s student affairs team plans to expand “support to help students adjust to college, build relationships, and navigate personal, social, or financial challenges,” she wrote.

The other Southern Illinois University campus, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, also saw historic growth this year.

University of Alabama in Huntsville

UAH’s total enrollment had been declining for half a decade before its turnaround this fall, when it increased by about 2 percent, though numbers won’t be finalized until October. That growth is the result of years of administrative changes, according to Michael Poll, UAH’s inaugural vice provost for enrollment management. In early 2025, the institution created his division, bringing together seven other offices, including admissions and veterans’ services, and launched an enrollment road map to try to address falling head count.

As part of that division’s work, Poll said, the institution dug into its scholarship data to get a better sense of how awards correlate with yield and retention. The team found that yield was much lower for students who hadn’t submitted test scores, so they gave a slight boost to the aid awarded to those students, resulting in a 5 percent yield increase. They also offered new scholarships for some transfer students and loosened scholarship renewal requirements after noticing how many students transferred out when they were at risk of losing their scholarship.

Poll said the university has also begun leveraging its proximity to the U.S. Space & Rocket Center and Space Camp, a popular children’s astronomy and astrophysics camp, offering small scholarships to all who attended the program. To attract students beyond Huntsville, UAH now has four dedicated regional recruiters in other parts of the country.

Though UAH’s gains weren’t massive this year, Poll said he’s hopeful the institution will continue its upward trajectory over the next three years of the strategic enrollment plan.

“It takes time to turn the ship around,” he wrote in an email. “It starts with one positive new enrollment year.”

Edward Waters University

The Jacksonville, Fla., HBCU has been on a steady increase over the past decade plus, nearly doubling its enrollment from a low of 751 students in 2011. But this year marked an important milestone: the institution’s highest enrollment—1,281—in two decades.

The university has expanded its academic programs and online education offerings significantly in recent years, growing from seven majors to 18, all of which are offered entirely online to appeal to adult learners and individuals outside the North Florida region; to help find those students, the institution works with a recruitment and marketing firm, which has nearly quintupled the university’s application volume since 2018. The expanded offerings include EWU’s first master’s programs, which came alongside a name change from Edward Waters College.

“The graduate programs did more than increase enrollment,” EWU President A. Zachary Faison Jr. told Inside Higher Ed in an email. “They changed how external audiences perceive this institution, including audiences that had never seriously considered us.”

But the institution is equally focused on its residential experience. It is currently working on building a new residence hall and a new track on campus, Faison said. And many transfer students, who have made up a significant portion of the institution’s enrollment increases in recent years, choose EWU because they are interested in moving from another four-year institution to the “smaller, family-like experience this campus offers,” he added.

Faison also sees athletics as an enrollment strategy; in 2024, EWU joined the NCAA in Division II, making it the only D2 HBCU in Florida.

Cape Fear Community College

After a few years of stagnant enrollment, CFCC earned a unique honor this year; of all North Carolina’s community colleges, it saw the biggest enrollment boom, with an 18 percent increase in full-time equivalency.

Like several other institutions that saw enrollment increases this year, CFCC recently established a new team dedicated to analyzing enrollment trends and data. Their efforts included a new initiative to reach out to students who had planned their courses but not registered. The institution also tackled some other hurdles for students, working aggressively to increase FAFSA completions by 16 percent and massively decreasing the number of students stuck on wait lists for courses they needed. A new student services team launched last year also focused on providing individualized support to incoming students to help them overcome any challenges in the enrollment process.

On the workforce front, the college expanded its quickest-turnaround short-term credential programs that are designed to get students into jobs as soon as possible, such as health care, truck driving and construction. It also continued building out its online offerings, which allow students across 46 U.S. states to study at CFCC.

Arkansas Tech University–Ozark

ATU–Ozark, a two-year college that has served as a branch campus of four-year Arkansas Tech since 2004, is projected to reach a record-high enrollment of 2,669 this year—the largest since 2014, with the strongest growth in health sciences and welding programs. In the past two years, enrollment across skilled-trade programs has surged 75 percent as students and families increasingly see the value of such credentials, according to Jessica Spicer, associate director of admissions at ATU–Ozark.

Spicer attributed the growth primarily to collaboration among campus partners.

“Our response to [enrollment] challenges has been to recognize that enrollment is a campus-wide responsibility,” she wrote in an email. “We developed an enrollment plan about a decade ago and have continued to work it, adjust it and stay committed to it. When we haven’t met a goal, we haven’t abandoned it. We’ve adjusted and kept working. That consistency has made a difference. Our current record enrollment is a reflection of the teamwork and collaboration across the institution and with the communities we serve.”

She also cited growing recruitment pipelines and partnerships with K–12 schools; the college now partners with 20 different schools on dual-enrollment programs, and concurrent enrollment skyrocketed 223 percent this year. Concurrent enrollment allows ATU–Ozark to connect earlier and in a more personalized manner with prospective students, showing them how accessible higher education can be, Spicer said.

University of California, Merced

California public higher education is a crowded field. But this year, after years of uneven enrollment, UC Merced, one of the less selective University of California campuses, saw a major increase in new students. The number of first-year students jumped 36 percent and transfers surged by 66 percent, bringing total enrollment to a record high of 9,647. The increase comes after enrollment dipped in fall 2025.

Administrators attributed the growth to several factors, including a slate of new majors focused on meeting workforce needs, such as accounting and computer science. The institution has also worked in recent years to increase its enrollment pipelines through a guaranteed admissions program that offers a simplified application to students from dozens of local schools and districts, as well as a streamlined transfer program for students at 16 community colleges.

Those pathways are meaningful at UC Merced, where 98 percent of students are in-state and the portion who come from the state’s Central Valley region, where the university is located, is growing.

Scott Hagg, vice chancellor of enrollment management, told Inside Higher Ed in an email that the university has been working to emphasize the assets that have long characterized a UC Merced education, including affordability, “a student-centered educational experience, opportunities for undergraduates to engage in research alongside faculty, a vibrant residential campus community, and the value of a University of California degree.”

title: Wellesley to Offer Free Tuition to Families Making Less Than $200K
summary:
Wellesley to Offer Free Tuition to Families Making Less Than $200K Olivia.sanchez Fri, 09/11/2026 - 03:00 AM Byline(s) Olivia Sanchez Wellesley to Offer Free Tuition to Families Making Less Than $200K
Olivia.sanchez Fri, 09/11/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
Wellesley College announced Wednesday it will offer free tuition to students from families that earn less than $200,000 per year, including typical assets such as home equity, investments and savings. The women’s liberal arts college in Massachusetts is the latest in a succession of institutions that have created promise programs to make higher education more accessible to students from low- and middle-income families.

“Wellesley’s mission of educating women of all socioeconomic backgrounds is more important than ever. Through the Wellesley Tuition Promise, we will open doors to more students, ensuring that cost is not an obstacle when it comes to a life-changing Wellesley education,” Wellesley President Paula Johnson said in a statement.

The tuition discount will be automatically applied for eligible incoming and returning students starting in fall 2027, the statement said. Their tuition will be covered by grants, according to the website.

Wellesley, which serves 2,300 students, historically funded most of its financial aid through its endowment. The Wellesley Tuition Promise program will be funded with money that became available due to changes to the college endowment tax rules, according to the statement.

Over the past few years, many colleges and universities have announced tuition-free college for families with incomes ranging from $75,000 to $200,000. Still, attending a college with such a program does not necessarily guarantee a $0 bill from the institution. While some colleges, such as Washington & Lee University in Virginia, offer free tuition to students from families making less than $150,000, plus free room and board for students whose families earn less than $75,000, Wellesley’s program is among those that don’t cover cost-of-living expenses or fees. The college estimates that even students eligible for free tuition will still be responsible for covering up to $26,000 for housing, food and a student activities fee, according to the statement.

T. Peaches Valdes, Wellesley’s dean of admission and financial aid, said in a statement that the program will remove the financial barrier to higher education for students from all backgrounds—including those from the roughly 86 percent of American households that bring in less than $200,000 per year.

“These students come to Wellesley because they want a rigorous education, and because they want to make a difference in the world. For an increasing number of students, Wellesley’s Tuition Promise will make that possible,” Valdes said.

title: Brooks and Capehart on the GOP's midterm identity
summary: David Brooks of The Atlantic and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW join Amna Nawaz to discuss the week in politics, including the GOP's midterm convention and the identity of the party, if Democrats should be worried about campaign spending benefiting Republican candidates and how America has changed in the 25 years since 9/11.
full_text:
Amna Nawaz:

For more on America 25 years after the 9/11 attacks and on the GOP Midterm Convention, we turn now to the analysis of Brooks and Capehart. That's "The Atlantic"'s David Brooks and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW.

It's good to see you both.

Jonathan Capehart:

Hey, Amna.

Amna Nawaz:

I want to put two things together this week and get your take on it.

We saw this week Republicans holding their midterm convention in Texas essentially built around President Trump, who asked people to take a pledge to him while on stage and promised $5,000 for every adult if Republicans win the midterms.

This week also marks one year since Charlie Kirk's assassination. This is someone who was sort of a bridge to the young conservative movement, hailed as the future of the Republican Party, a party now somewhat fractured on foreign policy and economic pressures, but really united around the president.

David, I want to ask you, if you put those two things together, what does it tell you about the identity of the party today?

David Brooks:

Yes, I thought the most important and, frankly, impressive speech, surprisingly for me, was Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s speech.

He really tried to describe why so many working-class voters who voted for his uncle and his dad in the '60s, then became Reagan Democrats under -- in the '80s, and then became Trump Republicans in 2016. And I certainly didn't agree with everything in that speech, but it was -- it was a very persuasive and to my Republican friends a very compelling story.

And that is the foundational strength of the modern Republican Party, that working-class shift. Now, as for the contemporary party, and Kennedy explicitly thanked -- why am I blanking out Turning Point USA guy?

Amna Nawaz:

Charlie Kirk.

David Brooks:

Charlie Kirk.

Amna Nawaz:

Sorry.

David Brooks:

Brain freeze.

For brokering the deal between Trump and him. And I would say we're seeing in the Republican Party first on the influencer side a crack-up. And so you got Candace going over to here, Tucker Carlson go over to here, Ben Shapiro trying to play William F. Buckley and police the movement and failing, by the way, though I admire him for trying.

Amna Nawaz:

Right.

David Brooks:

And so on that level, there's just like -- and that's like show business.

Among the Trump supporters I know, I would say there's exhaustion, disappointment, some sense of betrayal, but they're not turning Democrat. But they but they are -- they're flatter. They're emotionally flatter.

Amna Nawaz:

Yes.

David Brooks:

And then I think the long-term thing is, Donald Trump has -- with the exception of tariffs and immigration, he's undercut the intellectual consistency of the party, because he's all over the place on everything, including these $5,000, which is like super Keynesian pump priming at a time of inflation, which is like the worst thing you want to do.

So it's just intellectually incoherent. So that's a little complicated to say that the Republican still has a good story to tell.

Amna Nawaz:

Yes.

David Brooks:

They're cracking up on the ideological level, and then they're sort of adrift intellectually.

Amna Nawaz:

Jonathan, how do you look at this, and also the idea that this is someone, the president, who can boost the turnout, right? He can boost the base. He's starting to get more involved, deploying some of his significant PAC funds. Should Democrats be worried about that as you approach midterms?

Jonathan Capehart:

OK, where to begin.

Amna Nawaz:

OK.

Jonathan Capehart:

I will start with the money first.

Amna Nawaz:

OK.

Jonathan Capehart:

Yes, Democrats should be worried when there is a tsunami of cash that's coming in, in the last two months, and ad buys are popping up all over the place.

But I will tell you, Democrats have also been wide-eyed about their prospects. Even though the momentum seems to be going their way, even though there are incredible candidates in all of these races around the country, they have always known, particularly on the Senate side, that the map is really tough.

And so the fact that the president's actually going to spend his money in these races, good on him, but I think it's going to be tough for Democrats to match the money. But I would also say to Democrats and to others that money isn't everything. We have seen that in races around the country.

Angie Nixon had, what, less than a million dollars, and Mr. Vindman had six -- multiple millions, and she beat him by double digits in that primary race. So money isn't everything. Candidate quality can count for something, but money is something that is going to be hard to surmount.

And then, when it comes to the Republican Party, look, if you're holding a midterm convention and it's meant to boost turnout and meant to boost candidates around the country, and the president demands that he be center stage on both nights and pledge allegiance to him, great that Secretary Kennedy gave this great speech, but it would have been better if it had been coming from the president.

But that was never going -- that was never going to happen. And so this ideological drift that's happening within the Republican Party, I look forward to one day the Republicans going back to where they were under W., where they were under Reagan, because at least then there was consistency.

We knew what they stood for, we knew what the battle lines were, and you could talk and compromise. But you can't. And one last point on this, to your point about your friends being sort of emotionally flat. I have been hearing that from folks who live in some of these states where there used to be Trump signs everywhere, one person in Pennsylvania, another in Virginia, and I can't remember the other state.

But now these Trump signs are nowhere to be seen. And I think that speaks to a level of maybe disappointment, maybe betrayal that folks among Trump's faithful are feeling.

Amna Nawaz:

I do, while I have you both, want to spend a little time reflecting on this day. I know you both have been thinking deeply on it as well, but this moment as we are marking 25 years since those September 11 attacks.

David, how do you look back on your memories of that day and how we as a nation are different today than we were on September 10, 2001?

David Brooks:

Yes, well, I was in the air on when it all happened. I was flying to Sydney, Australia, and when we landed, the pilot said: "We haven't told you something, but this is not a joke. This really happened."

And they told us what had happened, and they said: "When you get off the jetway, there will be Qantas people with cell phones. They handed us phones, and they did everything they can to make us feel right. And what I mostly remember on that day is the taxi ride from the airport to the hotel.

My Australian taxi driver was weeping. And that was a sign of the world. Well, it's a sign of why you need allies, why you need friends, because that Australian guy was like one of us on that day. And there were people like that all around the world.

And when I look back 25 years hence, to me, that was the first day of the 21st century. And I mean that the al-Qaida did this thing. They sent the gyroscope oscillating, and then we overreacted in Iraq and Afghanistan, and then Putin is overreacting in Ukraine, and then October 7 happens, and then Israel responds.

So what we have just seen is like this gyroscope spinning wildly out of control. And it's like before World War -- I don't want to make that comparison too tightly, but it's like things are spinning out of control. The world feels ever more dangerous.

Amna Nawaz:

Jonathan, it's true. There was a world before, and there's a world after. How do you reflect on that?

Jonathan Capehart:

Well, on September 11, 25 years ago, today, it was primary day in New York City, and I had taken my first detour away from journalism and was working on Mike Bloomberg's first campaign for mayor.

And I left home, and I remember walking to the voting station, and I looked up at the sky, and it was and remains the most beautiful day I have ever seen. The sky was so blue. In my book, I wrote it was like New York City was domed by a sapphire.

And then we all know what happened next. It was a devastating day, absolutely devastating day for this -- for the people on those planes, for the people who passed away, their families, for the city, for the nation, for the world. The fact that the world came together -- I mean, Article 5 has only been invoked once, and that was for us, because we had been attacked.

We are a long way away from that world. I did an event last night at the Paley Center, and it wasn't until like the day before I realized, wait, I'm flying back on September 11. And a chill went through me, getting on a plane on September 11. I got to the airport this morning, and I got there just in time for them to be close up on the TSA line because they shut it down.

And I heard someone say, they're shutting it down because they're going to do a moment of silence. I got there about 8:30. Honor guard came in. It was silent. And I just -- my eyes just welled up with tears just remembering 25 years ago, those -- the people, their families, where we are now.

It is hard. It's really hard to think back what we were like on September 10, what we were like on September 11 at 8:30 a.m. in 2001, and where we are now. I pray we can maybe even get halfway back to that time. But I'm -- I don't know.

Amna Nawaz:

We are a long way from where we were, but hope springs eternal. And I thank you both for always being here to help us see some of that hope.

David Brooks, Jonathan Capehart, thank you so much.

Jonathan Capehart:

Thanks, Amna.

title: “We can’t just wait it out”: experts tout partnerships as antidote to compliance squeeze
summary:
International student policy shifts across the big four are not "a cycle we can simply wait out” and will force universities to rethink how they recruit, partner and design learning, sector leaders argued in a panel on international pathways and compliance.

The post “We can’t just wait it out”: experts tout partnerships as antidote to compliance squeeze appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The session, held at the InUni Global Convocation in central London last week, brought together voices from the US and UK to examine how institutions can protect opportunity for students while operating within increasingly constrained regulatory environments.

Kasia Krupka, associate director – UK partnerships & compliance at InUni Global, warned that the tightening of rules across major study destinations is both synchronised and systemic.

Looking accross stricter immigration controls in the UK, the US, Australia and Canada, “they’re all in the same boat and all points are going in the same direction”, she said.

“I don’t think it’s a cycle we can simply wait out,” she warned.

Her central question to the sector was blunt:

For Krupka, the answer lies in deeper knowledge of students – their intent, motivations and understanding of their chosen course – and in evidence‑based diversification rather than chasing headcount.

She pointed to the UK’s renewed – and tighter – Basic Compliance Assessment (BCA) metrics as an example: while one strand focuses on visas, the others focus on completion and outcomes.

“Those questions need to be asked a lot earlier than at the end of the journey,” she argued. “They need to be asked before the application comes into the funnel – through your partners, through your recruitment partners – to really understand the student that you’re recruiting.”

From a US perspective, Reitumetse Obakeng Mabokela, vice provost for global engagement at the University of Rochester, urged institutions to think about partnerships rather than mobility, especially in politically hostile or unpredictable environments.

She acknowledged the difficulty of convincing global partners that US institutions remain committed to international engagement.

“All you have to do is look at the news on any given day and say we’re not so sure about you,” she noted, adding that inhospitable immigration policies are a real constraint for US universities.

Yet she argued that this makes the quality of partnerships even more important. “If my colleague and my favorite partner in another university come together, we do some fabulous things, and then we each leave, then the relationship dies,” she pointed out.

Sometimes some partners are created more equal than others

Reitumetse Obakeng Mabokela, University of Rochester

She called on the sector to confront power and resource differentials in global collaboration. “Sometimes some partners are created more equal than others,” she said. “If we’re being truly collaborative partners, we have to engage that elephant in the room.”

From Teesside University, director of international development George Hunt stressed that in a world of tightening rules and rising scepticism about the value of university, student benefit must be the test for any international model – from TNE and articulation to joint degrees and credit mobility.

“Any partnership, any arrangement that a university has anywhere in the world, I think loses value very quickly if it isn’t valid for the student,” he said.

Sanjay Ramdath, vice president for enrolment management at the Borough of Manhattan Community College, framed his institution’s mission starkly.

“We take all students as they are. It’s our job to uplift them into where they want to be.”

He stressed that for many families, the key question is value and return on investment:

“What makes your degree from X school different than the degree from Y school? Because at the end, I need to know that that degree allows me to go in and get an interview, not a job… Can I even just walk in and get an interview?”

title: More choice matters only when students can navigate it
summary:
As student choice expands, technology and collaboration can help make international education pathways clearer, more connected and more meaningful, writes TOEFL's Omar Chihane.

The post More choice matters only when students can navigate it appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Consider a student in Ho Chi Minh City beginning her search for a university abroad. Her options may look very different from those available to a student making the same decision a decade ago.

Alongside long-established destinations such as Australia, the UK or the US, she may now be looking at South Korea, Japan or other growing education hubs closer to home.

That expansion of choice is one of international education’s great successes. It has also made the decision-making process more complicated.

Students are weighing changing visa policies, rising costs, new study destinations, employment prospects and an enormous amount of information. Institutions face a related challenge as they try to reach students who are likely to thrive in their programs, including those in markets they may not traditionally have served.

For our sector, the next phase of student mobility is about making those choices easier to navigate and more meaningful.

Today, the student journey is still surprisingly fragmented. Test preparation and assessment may happen in one place, university research in another, followed by applications, financing, admissions and enrollment through an entirely different set of systems.

Along the way, counselors, advisers, agents and institutions provide essential guidance. Yet the information available to them does not always connect as easily as it could.

Bringing more of that information together can create a clearer path for students. It can help them discover institutions, programs and destinations they may never have considered and better understand how those opportunities align with their skills, ambitions and circumstances.

It can also help institutions see talent in places they may not previously have reached.

Technology has an important role to play in making those connections possible. AI can help surface relevant opportunities and bring together information that would otherwise be difficult for a student or adviser to navigate alone. Its value, though, depends on how it is used.

International education is deeply personal. A decision to study abroad can involve family expectations, finances, career aspirations and a willingness to move thousands of miles from home. No technology can fully understand all of those considerations.

That is why human judgment, trust and transparency remain so important. From my perspective, the most promising use of technology is one that gives students and the people advising them a clearer picture of the opportunities available, while leaving the decision where it belongs; with the student.

The most promising use of technology is one that gives students and the people advising them a clearer picture of the opportunities available, while leaving the decision where it belongs; with the student.

This thinking is also reflected in ETS’s recent partnership with Passage. By connecting trusted TOEFL and GRE assessment insights with Passage’s matching and engagement technology, we are looking at how institutions can more effectively connect with students whose strengths and goals align with their programs, while helping students move more easily from discovery through enrollment. ETS continues to maintain its role in the development, delivery, scoring, security and research behind its assessments.

Progress will also depend on collaboration across the international education community. Institutions, counselors, agents, assessment organizations and technology providers each bring a different perspective and different expertise. Students benefit when those pieces work together more effectively.

Think again about that student in Ho Chi Minh City. Success is not simply giving her a longer list of universities to consider. It is helping her discover opportunities she may have missed, understand why they could be right for her and make a decision with confidence alongside the people she trusts.

International education has always been built on connections between countries, cultures, institutions and people. As the map of global mobility continues to change, strengthening those connections can help turn an abundance of choice into something much more valuable: a clearer sense of possibility.

About the author: As the general manager (GM) of TOEFL, Omar Chihane drives the strategic direction and growth of the TOEFL iBT, using his global experience as a tech entrepreneur and executive to lead teams across various functional areas of the business.

Prior to joining ETS in 2024, Omar founded englease – an English teaching startup that serves the Middle East and Africa through synchronous online classes. Before his startup journey, Omar held various leadership roles with multinational corporations including Siemens, Nokia and Microsoft. Omar holds an MBA from the London Business School and is a venture partner with Antler, where he coaches and mentors up and coming tech startups.

title: Microsoft Report Highlights Trends in Higher Education AI Adoption
summary:
Artificial Intelligence use in higher education continues to be hotly debated, but there’s no doubt it’s widely used: About 9 in 10 students, educators and education leaders say they’ve already used AI for school. That comes from Microsoft’s third annual AI in Education Special Report, which examines how K–12 districts and higher education institutions are adopting and using AI.
The report consolidates survey results from more than 3,000 instructors, education leaders and students in K–12 and higher education environments around the world. The findings go beyond who is using AI in education…
full_text:
Students, Educators and Leaders Have Different Views on AI Support

According to Microsoft’s findings, more than half of education leaders are using AI daily. Among students and teachers, however, the number is lower: About one-third of teachers and one-quarter of students use it every day in their school-related work. Many educators are using AI tools to brainstorm, plan lessons and simplify complex topics, while leaders are using it to work more efficiently and analyze data to improve students’ learning.

But while many institutions are encouraging AI use, there appears to be a big perception gap. Among survey respondents, 4 in 5 education leaders say their institution’s AI guidance is clear, but half of students and teachers say that guidance is nonexistent or neutral. To feel more supported and confident with AI, students and instructors say they need regular training; ideally; monthly or quarterly.

That’s likely a gap that leaders don’t realize they’re overlooking: 7 in 10 education leaders say at least half their students and instructors have had AI training. Conversely, 77% of students and 53% of educators say they have not had any formal AI training. That could be due to the speed of AI’s evolution.

“Education leaders say they’re delivering the content, but the end audience says they’re not receiving it. That deserves a closer look,” says Mark Sparvell, director of marketing education for Microsoft, in the report. “AI is changing so fast that people may not have time to embed what they’ve learned into their practice before it’s changed again, so they’re constantly feeling in deficit.”

To meet this need, schools must build practical AI literacy that withstands constant changes. This can mean ongoing, hands-on education opportunities, co-ops that allow educators to share with and learn from their peers, and short, stackable learning modules that can be completed even when time is tight.

Microsoft Offers AI Literacy Tools

Along with the report, Microsoft unveiled expanded AI tools tailored for education so schools can provide the kind of support and ongoing learning that students and educators need.

“Schools are places that develop skills — but they’re also where society itself is created,” Sparvell says. “AI gives educators an incredible range of new tools to accomplish that work.”

The new tools include:

Instructor tools that allow educators to brainstorm and plan standards-aligned lesson plans in minutes, set guidelines for how and when AI can be used in assignments and oversee student activity and lesson progression

Student tools that help students explore their classroom materials and use Copilot Chat as a research partner

Training through Microsoft Elevate for Educators, including a no-cost AI literacy program for educators and leaders looking to build confidence and transform classroom learning.

Microsoft offers a proof point from the University of South Carolina that tells how such AI tools can improve student learning, staff efficiency and the institution’s bottom line. After deploying Microsoft 365 Copilot for IT teams and students, more than 8 in 10 users reported saving one to five hours each week.

“On some weeks when I have to do a lot of work on my computer, Copilot might be saving me four or five hours in a week easily,” says Juan Caicedo, professor of civil and environmental engineering at the university. “Now I can spend that time with students.”

title: HFD-Monitor 2026: Personalisiertes Lernen im KI-Zeitalter
summary: Der neue Blickpunkt „Personalisiertes Lernen im KI-Zeitalter” stellt die zentralen Ergebnisse einer aktuellen Befragung von Vizepräsident*innen und Prorektor*innen Lehre zum Stand der...
full_text:
Auf strategischer Ebene beschäftigen sich Hochschulen mit der Personalisierung und Flexibilisierung im Kontext der Digitalisierung von Studium und Lehre, allerdings eher mit mittlerer Priorität: Während für 83 Prozent der Hochschulen die Vorbereitung der Studierenden auf eine KI- und digital geprägte Lebens- und Arbeitswelt im Kontext der Digitalisierung von Studium und Lehre ein strategisch sehr wichtiges Ziel ist, geben dies für das Thema Individualisierung/Personalisierung nur 34 Prozent an.

Spezifische Lerntechnologien und -szenarien, wie beispielsweise adaptives Lernen, lernbegleitendes Feedback und Selbstlernkurse stehen auch auf der strategischen Agenda. Allerdings berichten beispielsweise nur 14 Prozent, dass adaptive Lernsysteme an ihrer Hochschule (weitestgehend) verbreitet sind. Gleichzeitig wird dem Thema eine sehr hohe strategische Relevanz zugesprochen: 92 Prozent der Befragten stufen Adaptives Lernen als „eher relevant“ oder „sehr relevant“ ein. Dies deutet darauf hin, dass Adaptives Lernen für Hochschulen ein wichtiges Zukunftsthema ist, auch wenn die praktische Umsetzung vielerorts noch am Anfang steht.

Bei Learning Analytics und KI-Chatbots passiert schon mehr auf der Umsetzungsebene: 43 Prozent der befragten Hochschulen stellen Learning Analytics als Infrastruktur für personalisiertes Feedback an Studierende im Regel- oder Pilotbetrieb bereit. KI-gestützte Lernassistenten sind an 53 Prozent der befragten Hochschulen in der Umsetzung. Dies macht deutlich, dass (generative) Künstliche Intelligenz das Feld, was Lerntechnologien angeht, „von hinten aufräumt“ und neue Möglichkeiten für die Realisierung personalisierter Lernprozesse an deutschen Hochschulen schafft.

Hintergrund der Befragung

Der Blickpunkt gibt einen Überblick über die Ergebnisse des HFD-Fokusmonitors 2026. In dieser Reihe macht das HFD Trends und Themen des digitalen Wandels in Studium und Lehre an deutschen Hochschulen transparent, evidenzbasiert und ganzheitlich sichtbar. Im Gegensatz zum Monitor Digitalisierung 360° wird für den HFD-Fokusmonitor jeweils nur eine Zielgruppe befragt, um einen Einblick zu speziellen Fragestellungen zu bekommen. Die diesjährige Fokusbefragung widmet sich dem Thema personalisiertes Lernen. Befragt wurden Vizepräsident*innen/Prorektor*innen für Lehre aller deutschen Hochschulen zwischen Mai und Juni 2026.

title: Congreso Internacional de Revistas Universitarias
summary:
Edición Argentina - Del 6 al 9 de octubre

La entrada Congreso Internacional de Revistas Universitarias se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
La Universidad Provincial de Córdoba (UPC), Argentina, a través de su Secretaría de Ciencia, Arte y Tecnología, será la anfitriona del “Congreso Internacional de Revistas Universitarias (CIRU) – Edición Argentina”, que se realizará en las diferentes sedes de sus instalaciones y en universidades de Brasil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, España, entre otros, del 6 al 9 de octubre bajo una modalidad híbrida, permitiendo la participación presencial en las diferentes sedes de la UPC y la conexión virtual sincrónica para quienes participen de manera virtual, con participación del Consejo Latinoamericano de Ciencias Sociales.

Las revistas universitarias son un componente fundamental del ecosistema científico y académico, un espacio vital para la difusión del conocimiento. Estas publicaciones constituyen un canal de comunicación sustantivo para que investigadores/as, docentes y estudiantes puedan compartir sus trabajos y descubrimientos con la comunidad científica, el mundo productivo y el público en general.

Organizan: Universidad Provincial de Córdoba / Universidad Católica de Oriente / Universidade Estadual do Ceará, Brasil / Universidad Austral de Chile / Universidad Católica Silva Henríquez, Chile / Universidade Estadual do Sudoeste da Bahía, Brasil / CLACSO / Universidad Técnica Nacional / Oficina de Conocimiento Abierto – UNC / UNC Ciencia y Tecnología.

Ejes temáticos:

1. Innovación en la Gestión Editorial

2. Acceso Abierto y Políticas de Publicación

3. Ética y Buenas Prácticas en la Publicación Académica

4. Impacto y Evaluación de Revistas Académicas

5. De la Divulgación Científica a la Comunicación de la Ciencia y del Conocimiento

Modalidades de Participación e Inscripciones

El CIRU se desarrolla en modalidad híbrida (presencial en la Universidad Provincial de Córdoba y virtual), permitiendo diversas formas de involucramiento para editores/as, autores/as, investigadores/as, docentes, estudiantes y otros interesados. Las actividades siguen la consigna de “hacer, producir y poner manos a la obra”, fomentando la colaboración, experimentación y transferencia de conocimiento.

title: Las periferias del trabajo
summary:
Presentación viernes 18 de septiembre

La entrada Las periferias del trabajo se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
CLACSO, CEIL-CONICET, CIECS-CONICET-UNC y la Universidad Complutense de Madrid invitan a la presentación virtual del libro “Las periferias del trabajo”, coordinado por Hernán M. Palermo y María Lorena Capogrossi, el viernes 18 de septiembre.

Palabras de apertura: Fernanda Pampín (Directora de Producción Editorial de CLACSO)

Presentan:

–Hernan M. Palermo (CEIL-CONICET, Argentina)

–Lorena Capogrossi (CIECS-CONICET/UNC, Argentina)

Comentan:

–Sharryn M. Kasmir (Hofstra University, Estados Unidos)

–Pablo López Calle (Universidad Complutense de Madrid, España)

11.00 hs (Argentina / Brasil) / 10.00 hs (Cuba / República Dominicana) / 09.00 hs (Colombia / México)

Zoom | Transmisión en vivo por el canal de YouTube de CLACSO

“Las periferias del trabajo” reúne investigaciones provenientes de América, Europa y Asia en torno a problematizar el mundo del trabajo en el capitalismo contemporáneo. A través de un diálogo interdisciplinario, el texto da cuenta que las periferias no son una excepción, sino una condición estructural y en expansión que atraviesa geografías, sectores y sujetos.

El actual momento histórico revela un desplazamiento estructural del centro de gravedad del sistema-mundo hacia Oriente. Este desplazamiento implica una transformación profunda en las lógicas de acumulación y en la división internacional del trabajo. En ese reordenamiento, los procesos de periferización desbordan la clásica divisoria norte-sur y se instalan como una condición que ya no reconoce fronteras fijas ni geografías estables. Además, estas nuevas lógicas son acompañadas por la producción de poblaciones neoliberalizadas sobre las que se apuntalan los procesos de valorización del capital.

Este libro materializa una apuesta colectiva por producir herramientas críticas capaces de comprender las dinámicas laborales actuales y los desafíos que enfrenta la clase trabajadora.

CLACSO, CEIL-CONICET, CIECS-CONICET-UNC and the Complutense University of Madrid invite you to the virtual presentation of the book “The peripheries of work”, coordinated by Hernán M. Palermo and María Lorena Capogrossi, on Friday, September 18.

Opening words: Fernanda Pampín (Director of Editorial Production at CLACSO)

They present:

–Hernan M. Palermo (CEIL-CONICET, Argentina)

–Lorena Capogrossi (CIECS-CONICET/UNC, Argentina)

They comment:

–Sharryn M. Kasmir (Hofstra University, United States)

–Pablo López Calle (Complutense University of Madrid, Spain)

11:00 a.m. (Argentina / Brazil) / 10:00 a.m. (Cuba / Dominican Republic) / 9:00 a.m. (Colombia / Mexico)

Zoom | Live broadcast on the CLACSO YouTube channel

“The peripheries of work” brings together research from America, Europe and Asia to problematize the world of work in contemporary capitalism. Through an interdisciplinary dialogue, the text realizes that the peripheries are not an exception, but rather a structural and expanding condition that crosses geographies, sectors and subjects.

The current historical moment reveals a structural shift of the center of gravity of the world-system towards the East. This shift implies a profound transformation in the logic of accumulation and the international division of labor. In this reordering, the processes of peripheralization go beyond the classic north-south divide and are established as a condition that no longer recognizes fixed borders or stable geographies. Furthermore, these new logics are accompanied by the production of neoliberalized populations on which capital valorization processes are underpinned.

This book materializes a collective commitment to produce critical tools capable of understanding current labor dynamics and the challenges faced by the working class.

title: La Política Exterior Feminista en la Agenda Parlamentaria
summary:
Equipo docente: Michael Hardt y Sandro Mezzadra

La entrada La Política Exterior Feminista en la Agenda Parlamentaria se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
COORDINACIÓN: Marita Perceval – Nora Goren

Duración: 1 mes

Destinatarias/os: Parlamentarios y parlamentarias, integrantes y asesores/as de la Comisión de Igualdad de Género, Niñez y Juventud y de la Comisión de Asuntos Políticos, Municipales y de la Integración del PARLATINO.

El curso pretende fortalecer las capacidades de parlamentarias, parlamentarios, asesoras y asesores del PARLATINO para incorporar la perspectiva y asuntos prioritarios de la Política Exterior Feminista en la agenda legislativa regional y contribuir al fortalecimiento del sistema multilateral y a la construcción de una gobernanza internacional justa, democrática, inclusiva, representativa, igualitaria, multicultural, respetuosa del derecho internacional y comprometida con los derechos humanos, a nivel regional y global.

El aporte de las mujeres de América Latina y el Caribe a la política exterior y a las relaciones internacionales: genealogía del multilateralismo desde las voces del Sur Global.

La participación de las mujeres en las instituciones diplomáticas a nivel nacional, regional y global: De la masculinidad hegemónica a la creciente presencia de las mujeres en el ámbito de las relaciones internacionales.

Voces y propuestas del movimiento de mujeres en AL en las cinco conferencias gubernamentales de Política Exterior Feminista (Berlín, Países bajos, Francia, México, España.

Democracias paritarias para un desarrollo sostenible con justicia económica, social y ambiental: La Recomendación General 40 de la CEDAW y los aportes de la PEF

Marcos legislativos y principios orientadores para el desarrollo de sistemas integrales de cuidados, políticas de igualdad de género, corresponsabilidad social y autonomía de las mujeres. Avances y desafíos en América Latina y el Caribe.

Instrumentos regionales y globales como el Compromiso de Buenos Aires, el Compromiso de Tlatelolco, la Opinión Consultiva 31/25, las resoluciones pertinentes del Consejo de Derechos Humanos y de la Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas (entre ellas, las resoluciones A/HRC/RES/54/6, A/HRC/RES/55/8, A/RES/77/317 y E/RES/2024/4), la Ley Modelo Interamericana de Cuidados y su Guía de Implementación (CIM/OEA, 2022 y 2023), la Declaración Conjunta sobre el Pacto Birregional por los Cuidados UE–ALC (2025) y otros documentos estratégicos.

Bases normativas y principios rectores para una economía del cuidado con justicia fiscal e inclusión social desde una perspectiva decolonial, interseccional, multicultural, despatriarcalizadora, no-capacitista, y antieconomicista (Consenso de Montevideo sobre Población y Desarrollo, el Compromiso de Buenos Aires, el Consenso de Santo Domingo, el Consenso de Santiago, la Estrategia de Montevideo para la Implementación de la Agenda Regional de Género, la Declaración y Plataforma de Acción de Beijing, la Agenda 2030, el Pacto para el Futuro, el Compromiso de Sevilla y las resoluciones pertinentes del Consejo de Derechos Humanos de las Naciones Unidas sobre el derecho al desarrollo).

Reorientación y fortalecimiento del financiamiento y la cooperación internacional: del asistencialismo de los donantes al financiamiento sustentable y la cooperación corresponsable.

Intersectorialidad e interseccionalidad: puentes epistémicos y articulaciones estratégicas entre el sector académico y los parlamentos.

Geopolítica de la fragmentación y minilateralismos en disputa: la gobernanza de los bienes comunes y globales en un nuevo orden mundial anclado en procesos innovadores de integración regional (bienes comunes globales y bienes públicos globales desarrolladas por Naciones Unidas en Nuestra Agenda Común (2021), analizando sus implicancias para la gobernanza internacional, el financiamiento del desarrollo y la cooperación multilateral).

La diplomacia parlamentaria en la Agenda del Futuro y el Compromiso de Sevilla como componentes clave de las agendas prioritarias a nivel regional y global (estrategias y mecanismos de diplomacia parlamentaria en espacios multilaterales regionales y globales. En ese marco, se promoverá una articulación con el grupo GRULAC de la UIP y se trabajará con documentos como la Guía para la práctica parlamentaria, el Manual sobre la CEDAW y las herramientas de autoevaluación elaboradas por la Unión Interparlamentaria (UIP)).

Se propone realizar una sesión especial de cierre que recupere los principales debates desarrollados durante el curso y reflexione sobre los desafíos de la Política Exterior Feminista para la región.

Marita Perceval

Nora Goren

Antonia Urrejola Noguera

Yanerit Cristina Morgan Sotomayor

Constanza Moreira

Ana Güezmes

Bibiana Aído

Desiree del Rosario

María Cristina Perceval

El curso está compuesto por tres módulos, de una hora de duración cada uno, con clases grabadas y materiales complementarios y un cierre virtual sincrónico.

Los y las participantes tendrán además acceso a recursos bibliográficos seleccionados, disponibles en el aula virtual, que acompañarán y profundizarán los contenidos y debates trabajados durante las clases.

title: Nuovo stabilimento per Clivet dedicato al mercato europeo
summary: Frutto di un investimento di 24 milioni prosegue il percorso di sviluppo delle tecnologie per la climatizzazione nel terziario
full_text:
È iniziata la produzione nel nuovo stabilimento Clivet a Feltre dedicato alla produzione di pompe di calore e soluzioni per la climatizzazione ad alta efficienza per applicazioni nel terziario con l’impiego di refrigeranti naturali. Frutto di un investimento di 24 milioni la struttura si sviluppa su una superficie di 14mila metri quadri, rafforza la filiera industriale del territorio e al momento impiega 80 addetti, di cui 50 impiegate nella produzione e i restanti sono colletti bianchi, ed è già stato previsto un piano di nuove assunzioni sulla base dello sviluppo del mercato. «L’apertura del nuovo stabilimento di Feltre rappresenta un passaggio strategico nel percorso di crescita di Clivet - ha detto Stefano Bellò, presidente e Ceo di Clivet -. Abbiamo scelto di investire nel nostro territorio per garantire il tempestivo sviluppo delle soluzioni richieste dal mercato europeo, aumentare la capacità produttiva tanto nel riscaldamento quanto nelle tecnologie del raffrescamento e mettere a disposizione di clienti e partner sistemi capaci di coniugare comfort, efficienza energetica e sostenibilità».

Lo stabilimento è un altro passo in seno al percorso di espansione che Clivet sta guidando all’interno di Mbt Climate, la divisione europea e house of brands di Midea building technologies (Gruppo Midea) che ha portato prima alla realizzazione dell’Innovation Centre di Padova, punto di riferimento internazionale per la ricerca e sviluppo nel mercato Hvac, acronimo inglese di riscaldamento, ventilazione e condizionamento dell’aria, inaugurato la scorsa estate, ed ora del nuovo stabilimento di Feltre, che ne rappresenta lo sviluppo industriale a sostegno degli ambiziosi obiettivi europei in materia di carbon neutrality e sostenibilità. «In termini di capacità produttiva, il nuovo impianto a pieno regime sarà in grado di produrre 8.800 unità all’anno, raddoppiando la capacità attuale per le specifiche linee – prosegue Bellò –. La forte spinta per i prodotti Clivet nel terziario e lo sviluppo di nuovi mercati all’orizzonte vedrà il 70% della sua produzione con una destinazione estera, in particolar modo verso i mercati del Centro-Nord Europa, dove la richiesta di pompe di calore per la decarbonizzazione nel settore terziario è in continua crescita». Tra le altre cose lo stabilimento è dotato delle più avanzate tecnologie ad alta efficienza energetica e basso impatto ambientale: sul tetto dell’edificio c’è un impianto fotovoltaico da 1.008 pannelli per una potenza totale di 805 KWp, che permette di coprire 67% dei consumi, con una stima di autoconsumo dell’87% e quindi ci sarà anche un apporto di energie alla rete.

«L’avvio del nuovo stabilimento è il risultato di un intenso lavoro di progettazione, realizzazione e organizzazione industriale - sottolinea Marco Bertazzo, plant manager di Clivet -. Abbiamo sviluppato le linee applicando i principi della lean manufacturing, con l’obiettivo di creare flussi più efficienti, eliminare gli sprechi e concentrarci sulle attività che generano valore per il cliente. Abbiamo inoltre progettato le linee per integrare robot e robot collaborativi, veicoli a guida autonoma in un’ottica di automazione collaborativa. Abbiamo anche deciso di investire sul piano delle competenze e del capitale umano: vogliamo attrarre e formare professionalità capaci di accompagnare l’evoluzione tecnologica del settore e offrire nuove opportunità ai giovani del territorio». Per l’edificio Clivet ha richiesto la certificazione Leed Silver, leadership in energy and environmental design.
